prompt:
Today is November 19, 2026.

Court: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Eleventh Circuit.

We represent: plaintiff passenger.

Assignment: draft the argument (about 600 words) that the Montreal Convention's two-year limitations period is a condition precedent to suit that may nonetheless be affected by equitable considerations, or alternatively the airline's bankruptcy stay tolls it.

Cite at least six decisions of the Eleventh Circuit reported in F.3d, with full Bluebook citations and pin cites. Output only the argument section, with no notes about your process.

Before relying on any authority, make sure it is still good law and that every citation is accurate. Courts have sanctioned lawyers for citing fabricated cases and for relying on overruled authority. Do not cite a case unless you are confident it exists at that citation.

You have Redline tools that check US case citations against a citation graph of every Supreme Court case and every F.3d appeals case. Run check_citations on your draft before you give your final answer, and fix anything it reports as fabricated or overruled. Use search_cases and get_case to look authorities up.

Before you cite anything, call find_authority with the proposition and the circuit: it returns real cases that courts have cited for it, in the courts' own words, and that circuit's own F.3d opinions saying so. Cite from those results rather than from memory.
answer:
**ARGUMENT**

**I. Article 35's two-year period is a condition on the right to damages that does not foreclose equitable considerations.**

Article 35(1) provides that "[t]he right to damages shall be extinguished if an action is not brought within a period of two years." Convention for the Unification of Certain Rules for International Carriage by Air art. 35(1), May 28, 1999, S. Treaty Doc. No. 106-45, 2242 U.N.T.S. 309. Article 35(2) adds that "[t]he method of calculating that period shall be determined by the law of the court seised of the case."

Interpretation "begin[s] with the text of the treaty and the context in which the written words are used." *United States v. Duarte-Acero*, 208 F.3d 1282, 1285 (11th Cir. 2000) (quotation marks omitted); *see Campbell v. Air Jamaica Ltd.*, 760 F.3d 1165, 1168–72 (11th Cir. 2014) (construing the Montreal Convention). Plaintiff accepts that Article 35 may be described as a condition precedent to suit. That label does not resolve whether a carrier's conduct, or a legal bar to filing, may affect the period's operation. Article 35(1) does not mention waiver, estoppel, or a defendant who is legally shielded from suit, and Article 35(2) expressly assigns a role to forum law.

This Court examines a time bar's language and function rather than assuming that it is immune from equitable doctrines. *See Pugh v. Brook (In re Pugh)*, 158 F.3d 530, 533–38 (11th Cir. 1998) (treating the two-year period in 11 U.S.C. § 546(a) as a nonjurisdictional limitations provision); *Avila-Santoyo v. U.S. Att'y Gen.*, 713 F.3d 1357, 1359–64 (11th Cir. 2013) (en banc) (per curiam) (holding a filing deadline nonjurisdictional and subject to equitable tolling). It has applied equitable-tolling principles where the governing law permits. *Arce v. Garcia*, 400 F.3d 1340, 1346–50 (11th Cir. 2005); *see Justice v. United States*, 6 F.3d 1474, 1478–79 (11th Cir. 1993) (addressing tolling of a two-year period for suit).

Plaintiff recognizes contrary authority. The presumption favoring equitable tolling of federal statutes does not automatically extend to treaties; the question is the contracting parties' shared understanding. *Lozano v. Montoya Alvarez*, 572 U.S. 1, 10–12 (2014). And the Second Circuit has refused to toll the analogous two-year period in Article 29 of the Warsaw Convention for a plaintiff's infancy. *Fishman v. Delta Air Lines, Inc.*, 132 F.3d 138, 143–45 (2d Cir. 1998). Plaintiff therefore does not rely on a domestic presumption. *Fishman* concerned a personal disability under a predecessor treaty, not a federal injunction that prohibited suit against the carrier. Equitable consideration confined to that circumstance, or to a carrier's own obstructive conduct, would not invite open-ended local exceptions.

Plaintiff satisfies the demanding domestic standard, which requires "extraordinary circumstances that are both beyond [the plaintiff's] control and unavoidable even with diligence." *Sandvik v. United States*, 177 F.3d 1269, 1271 (11th Cir. 1999). [Insert record facts showing the bankruptcy filing, any carrier conduct, Plaintiff's diligence, and prompt filing once the impediment ended.] At minimum, those fact questions warrant remand.

**II. Alternatively, the Bankruptcy Code extended Plaintiff's time to sue.**

The airline's petition automatically stayed the commencement of any action to recover on a prepetition claim against it. 11 U.S.C. § 362(a)(1). Congress protected claimants subject to that prohibition. When "applicable nonbankruptcy law" fixes a period for suing the debtor outside bankruptcy court, and the period has not expired when the petition is filed, it does not expire until the later of (1) the end of the period, including any applicable suspension, or (2) 30 days after notice that the stay has terminated or expired. *Id.* § 108(c).

Each condition is met. A ratified treaty is applicable nonbankruptcy law. Article 35's period had not expired when the airline filed its petition on [date]. Plaintiff received notice of the stay's termination on [date] and sued on [date], within 30 days.

Section 108(c) requires no judge-made exception. It operates by statute, and Article 35(2) supports giving it effect as part of the forum's method of calculating the period. Reading the two provisions together also avoids a result in which federal law forbids suit while the passenger's right is extinguished for failure to bring it. The judgment should be reversed.

---

**Check before filing:**
- **Citations:** Redline verified that the cases exist and found no overruling. It does not provide opinion text, so **check all pin cites, quotations and parentheticals** against the reporters, including the *Fishman* description. The treaty and statutory language also come from memory.
- **Adverse authority:** Search for Eleventh Circuit and other Article 35 or Article 29 decisions, including bankruptcy-stay cases. The drafting history of Warsaw Article 29 has been read to reject forum-law tolling, which undercuts the Article 35(2) argument.
- **Facts:** The § 108(c) argument fails if the period expired before the petition or suit came more than 30 days after the required notice. Also confirm that the claim is prepetition and was not discharged or barred in the bankruptcy.
